item.title: My TV's underpowered USB port was driving me crazy until I discovered this simple fix
item.itunes:title: My TV's underpowered USB port was driving me crazy until I discovered this simple fix
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
TVs aren't exactly cutting-edge, and they rarely have inputs that can keep up with the latest, power-hungry peripherals. Most of the time, they don't even have enough power to run everything I plug into them. I've run into this problem often when plugging in a large hard drive that needs far more power than the TV can deliver. The TV might power on the accessory but drop the connection as power requirements increase.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

A powered USB hub offers a straightforward solution. Instead of relying on the TV to supply all the power, I can use a hub with its own power adapter. That way, connected accessories get a separate power source while the USB port handles data. It's that simple and can save you hours of troubleshooting.

Why your TV's USB port struggles to power external hard drives

A TV's USB port isn't designed for every accessory

First, you need to understand that not all USB ports are created equal. A port on a television might be perfectly fine for playing back files from a flash drive, but it can't supply enough power to every accessory. These ports, especially on televisions, are designed for simpler use cases, and their power output rarely meets the latest standards.

This is a big problem when you connect something like an external hard drive to your TV. Let's say you want to play back your ripped Blu-ray 4K collection on your big-screen TV. Depending on your setup, plugging in your hard drive is often the best approach. However, you might observe that the device starts to fail, disconnects unexpectedly, or doesn't work reliably. In some cases, the TV might recognize the accessory before it disappears.

Mechanical drives draw a fair amount of power when spinning up, and a TV's USB port often struggles to meet that demand. The result is an unreliable connection with all the signs I talked about above.

A powered USB hub addresses this limitation by bringing its own power adapter into the setup. I have to connect the hub to a compatible USB port on the TV, plug its power adapter into a wall outlet, and connect my accessories to the hub. The external power supply handles the power requirements of compatible connected devices instead of making them depend entirely on the TV's USB output.

This is different from using a regular USB hub. A standard USB hub has no power input and can't boost power to connected accessories. Instead, it pulls power from the host device, in this case, the TV, and shares it with connected accessories. If the TV is already struggling to power a single device, adding an unpowered hub can make things worse. A powered hub solves this.

I stopped charging my phone through my car's USB port after making one simple upgrade

I switched to a 12V USB-C charger in my car, and my phone never drains again

32
By  Dhruv Bhutani

A powered USB hub does more than add extra ports

Check compatibility first

The same principle applies if you want to connect multiple USB accessories simultaneously. Modern TVs usually provide a single USB 3.0 port. Using the single port for a hard drive leaves fewer options for other devices. For example, you might want to connect a keyboard or another hard drive. A powered hub can add ports, making it easier to organize your setup.

However, don't assume every accessory will work just because the hub has extra ports. The television still needs to support the device, while the hub handles the power. TV platforms are inherently limited, so just because you can plug in the device doesn't mean it'll work. In fact, the same limitations extend to hard drives and flash drives too. Keep the drive's file system in mind, because the TV might not support it out of the box.

Also, a powered hub isn't the right fix for every use case. If you're trying to power up a streaming stick that connects over HDMI, a powered hub isn't what you need. Instead, pair the streaming stick with a standard wall-powered adapter.

I connected my HD antenna to a cheap tuner, and now I can watch free TV anywhere in my house

With a refurbished tuner and HD Antenna, I get OTA live TV everywhere.

5
By  Brian Burgess

A powered USB hub is the easiest fix for an underpowered TV port

The fact is that a TV's USB port doesn't have to be powerful enough for every accessory I want to connect to it. Nor do I need to take the television in for troubleshooting because one device won't work as it should. A powered USB hub can provide the extra power compatible accessories need while giving you more USB connections.

The important part is identifying the actual problem before buying anything. If an accessory is struggling because the TV's USB port can't supply enough power, a powered hub is a simple solution worth considering. If the television doesn't support the accessory or the way it's connected, though, adding a hub won't magically fix it. Regardless, if USB disconnections are the problem you're facing, this is the first fix I'd recommend.

Sabrent 4-port USB Hub (HB-UM43)

item.title: Your ISP's router may be broadcasting a second Wi-Fi network for strangers
item.itunes:title: Your ISP's router may be broadcasting a second Wi-Fi network for strangers
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Millions of subscribers plug in an all-in-one gateway provided by a lot of major ISPs, assuming its wireless radios exclusively service their private household devices. However, if you scan local 2.4GHz and 5GHz RF channels, you will often reveal secondary open public networks originating from the exact same physical radio hardware and MAC address block, using separate BSSIDs. ISPs routinely turn residential gateway hardware into public Wi-Fi hotspots by default, while segmenting them at the logical network layer via VLANs. This practice consumes local wireless airtime, alters gateway thermal/power profiles, and can strip network control away from you.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
I finally made my Wi-Fi snappier by changing the most ignored setting on my router

Your router's transmit power isn't supposed to be at the maximum level

11
By  Tanveer Singh

ISPs try hard to stop guest affecting you

There is logical network segmentation

How do dual-BSSID Wi-Fi hotspots actually work? ISPs provide Wi-Fi hotspots to their customers, and a lot of the time this comes at the expense of the router that it's originating from, despite attempts from your ISP to ensure you don't notice.

Modern Wi-Fi access point chips assign multiple virtual access point interfaces, each with its own distinct BSSID and SSID, to a single physical 2.4GHz, 5GHz, or 6GHz wireless radio card. The router broadcasts separate beacon frames for your private network and the public ISP hotspot it's generating over the exact same physical antenna array and channel frequency.

There is logical network segmentation so traffic on the public guest SSID is isolated at Layer 2 using virtual local area networks or VLANs. Public client traffic doesn't hit your private subnet or local DHCP server. Instead, it's encapsulated in a GRE, or generic routing encapsulation, tunnel directly from the gateway back to the ISP's core network.

ISPs configure quality of service queues to prioritize private subscriber traffic over public guest traffic, so your traffic is always prioritized. Public usage is metered separately on the ISP side and doesn't count towards your monthly data cap, if you have one, though it does share the same physical coaxial or fiber WAN pipe.

But there are technical disadvantages

Your airtime is being hogged

There are some real technical disadvantages behind this happening. The first and most noticeable is airtime contention and channel coexistence. Wi-Fi relies on CSMA/CA, meaning carrier-sense multiple access with collision avoidance. This essentially means only one device can transmit on a specific frequency channel at a time. Even if public guest traffic is rate-limited at the WAN layer, strangers connected to your router still consume physical wireless airtime, which can increase packet contention and latency for your private devices on that same channel.

There's also unnecessary beacon overhead and co-channel interference, as every additional SSID broadcast requires continuous 102.4ms beacon frames sent at the lowest basic data rate, which is often 6Mbps. In dense housing or apartment complexes where dozens of ISP gateways broadcast multiple SSIDs, this creates severe beacon clutter and significantly reduces available channel capacity across the 2.4GHz and 5GHz spectrums.

And lastly, of course, are power draw, thermal loads, and memory reserves. Maintaining additional VAPs, managing public client association tables, and running continuous GRE tunnel encapsulation can significantly increase your router's processing overhead, especially for the Gateway System-on-Chip. This, as a result, will drive up internal device temperatures and background power consumption of your router.

Audit your network

And toggle off the feature

There is a way to actually audit and reclaim your local spectrum and avoid your ISP using your router in this specific way. Before starting, the first thing you want to do is perform an RF audit using a Wi-Fi analyzer. There is a range of network analyzer tools available on both iOS and Android devices that will help you inspect any local BSSIDs. Match the MAC address of your private Wi-Fi network against adjacent open SSIDs. If the MAC address matches, except for the last octet or vendor prefix, the public network is originating from your router.

Now that you know your router is being used in this way, the best next step is to disable guest or community hotspot features via your internet service provider's account portal. Because ISPs lock down local gateway firmware, turning off the public SSID often cannot be done without logging straight into your ISP's account portal. This is sometimes a web portal or a mobile app. Once you're in the settings, have a look at your advanced settings or your home hotspot settings and toggle off the public Wi-Fi/community hotspot feature.

While toggling off this setting should rectify the issue, if you want to go a step further, you can put the ISP gateway into full bridge mode (which will disable its routing, NAT, and Wi-Fi radios entirely). Then you can connect your own standalone router or access point running open networking stacks or dedicated local hardware to ensure absolute control over all of your radio broadcasts, channel widths, and network security. It's not essential, but it gives you an extra layer of protection.

Don't let strangers steal your airtime

Toggle off this network setting

Shared ISP community hotspots leverage customer-funded hardware and power to expand provider network footprints. While logically isolated from your private data, public Wi-Fi broadcasts unnecessarily consume wireless airtime, pollute the local RF environment, and complicate home network management. The best course of action is to audit your wireless spectrum, opt out of any provider-hosted public hotspots through your account portal, or bypass ISP gateway radios entirely by switching to dedicated personally owned networking hardware in bridge mode.

item.title: I replaced Firefox with Zen, and it's what Mozilla should have built years ago
item.itunes:title: I replaced Firefox with Zen, and it's what Mozilla should have built years ago
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The way we use the internet has changed drastically over the last few years. Watching hour-long YouTube videos has slowly given way to scrolling through TikTok and Instagram Reels. Googling every little question is no longer second nature when you can just ask ChatGPT. Building an app, something that once required weeks of learning to code, can now take a fraction of that time with AI.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Yet, despite how much our internet habits have changed (for better or for worse), one thing has remained surprisingly constant: the browser. Sure, we've seen plenty of AI-powered browsers pop up recently, but at their core, they're still browsers. That's why I think choosing the right browser is almost as important as picking the right shoes for a trip where you know you'll be walking 20,000 steps a day.

I've experimented with my fair share of browsers over the years, and Firefox was my go-to for a good chunk of that time. That was until I discovered Zen, a browser that made me wonder why Mozilla hadn't built something like it years ago.

Browsers have forgotten how to just be browsers

Every feature wants a piece of your screen

Now, I've tried practically every AI browser out there. While I do think they're more than a gimmick and have some truly useful features up their sleeve, I also think we've reached the point where we're going a tad bit overboard. I'm beginning to get somewhat annoyed by every app I use having AI scattered throughout it, especially in places it has no business being. My email client, the software I write my articles on, the tool I use to edit the images I take for my articles — practically everything I use has some sort of AI feature baked into it.

While I'm all for AI making my life easier, I don't need every tool I use to forcibly become an AI assistant. A browser is a prime example of that. If it has AI features, I'd rather they be tucked away so I can enable them when I actually need them, instead of having them shoved in my face every time I open a new tab.

item.itunes:summary:
A lot of the advice for getting better results from AI models comes from the companies running those models in data centers. Their documentation is pretty detailed and actually sensible for the most part, the issue is that a lot of local LLM guides end up repeating that same advice. But local AI on an 8GB GPU can't be tuned or used the same as a hefty Claude model on Anthropic's servers. After having run local LLMs for real work for the better part of this year, I realized the tweaks and tricks often go against the grain of what cloud providers recommend.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Keeping "Thinking" turned off

The feature cloud models brag about is the one I turn off first

Thinking, or reasoning mode, is when a model writes out its work before giving you an answer. The idea is that it's meant to be more accurate on complex tasks. Most of my models have a thinking mode, including my Qwen, Gemma 4, and Qwythos models.

Cloud providers lean hard on the thinking thing, to the point where some won't even let you opt out. Claude Opus 5.5 runs with thinking permanently on, and Google says every Gemini 3.x model always thinks too, so the closest you get is turning the effort down. OpenAI does let developers set GPT-5.5's reasoning effort to none, but the default is medium, and OpenAI only suggests dropping it if you want a quick reply more than a clever one.

I keep Thinking off on pretty much all my local models, and context is the main reason. My runner's context window has to hold everything, meaning my prompt, the conversation history, any files I added, and also the model's thinking. Keeping it turned off is basically like a budgeting hack for a bit of extra savings. It legitimately saves me a few hundred up to a thousand tokens per prompt. Any prompt that really needed thinking that badly was going to go to my cloud models anyway because that's still what I reach for with complex or multi-step tasks.

I'm not paying $20 for ChatGPT or Claude because a free local LLM does everything I need

The bills disappeared, but the job gets done all the same

19
By  Abhinav Raj

Switching on Min P sampling

A setting cloud users have never even been offered

Min P is a sampling setting, so it changes how the model picks each next word. It sets a minimum cutoff that scales with how likely the model's top choice is, then throws out the long tail of unlikely words underneath it. This is an excellent setting to turn up when you have a high temperature (more random than analytical) because it basically prevents the model from going a little off the rails. Whenever my temp is over 0.3, I bump up Min P between 0.03 and 0.05.

Cloud tools don't offer it at all - OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google don't expose Min P as a setting, and the bigger trend is that they don't expose these sampling controls at all. Claude Sonnet 5 rejects any non-default temperature or top P value, and Anthropic tells developers to use prompting instead. OpenAI and Google aren't much different. GPT-5.5 only accepts the default temperature, and while Google still lets you change it on Gemini 3, it strongly recommends sticking to 1.0 because lower values can cause looping.

For what it's worth, Qwen's own recommended settings leave Min P at 0.0, but I still keep it on whenever I have a higher temperature because it prevents replies from becoming unusable.

I replaced ChatGPT and Claude with this powerful local LLM and saved over $20 a month while gaining full control

Qwen3.6 runs on my old GPU and does what ChatGPT does for free

27
By  Ayush Pande

Capping the context window

Cloud models brag about millions of tokens, I keep mine very low

Context length is how many tokens a model can hold at once. Like I've already mentioned, everything counts towards it, including your prompts, files, and the model's responses. Cloud models have pushed that number past a million, with GPT-5.5 sitting just above 1M and Claude Sonnet 5 serving a 1M window by default. Anthropic even publishes tips specifically for individual prompts carrying 20k tokens of documents.

What's interesting is that Anthropic's own context engineering guide warns about context rot, which is when recall gets worse when the window starts filling up. This happens a lot sooner with local models if you don't have a massive card, which is why I keep my context around 30k usually. I can get it running smoothly on up to 80k, but I need to account for other apps I'm running at the same time as well, which I usually am, especially when a local model is plugged into a design tool or agentic workspace.

My models technically go way higher - Qwen 3.5 9B supports 262k natively, but that's just not an option for my GPU. A lower context window is actually not that limiting. It forces you to really think through your prompts and be selective with what to add to a session. It can get a bit restrictive when I'm trying to do multi-step tasks though.

I ran GLM 5.3, a 744-billion-parameter model, on my home lab, and the frontier suddenly feels a lot closer

1.5TB of model, 350GB of computer. Math shouldn't work like this.

15
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Reaching for a smaller model first

The advice to start big doesn't matter when your GPU is small

Cloud providers usually tell you to start big. OpenAI's model selection guide says to begin with the most capable model and only test smaller ones once cost and latency become more relevant. And Anthropic says most workloads should start with Claude Opus 5.5. I mean, this is probably mainly marketing - of course every AI company wants you to try their most capable models so the cheaper ones end up feeling like a downgrade.

When it comes to local AI, I start small intentionally; usually Gemma E2B, E4B, or Qwen 3.5 4B. It simply comes down to conserving system resources - if those models can handle the task fine, why even bother scaling up? Qwen 3.5 4B gets all my tiny coding jobs like fixing little buttons, and my Gemma models get my quick chats.

My local LLM can call Claude when it's stuck, and it changed everything about my local-first setup

Local LLMs aren't very good on their own

14
By  Anurag Singh

My little GPU plays by different rules

Cloud guides are written with data centers in mind, and they don't really account for a model squeezed onto an 8GB card that also needs to run a notes app, a browser, and an image editor. I think the more useful habit is treating every default like a suggestion, then poking at it on your own hardware and deciding what actually works for your setup.

Thinking, or reasoning mode, is when a model writes out its work before giving you an answer. The idea is that it's meant to be more accurate on complex tasks. Most of my models have a thinking mode, including my Qwen, Gemma 4, and Qwythos models.

Cloud providers lean hard on the thinking thing, to the point where some won't even let you opt out. Claude Opus 5.5 runs with thinking permanently on, and Google says every Gemini 3.x model always thinks too, so the closest you get is turning the effort down. OpenAI does let developers set GPT-5.5's reasoning effort to none, but the default is medium, and OpenAI only suggests dropping it if you want a quick reply more than a clever one.

I keep Thinking off on pretty much all my local models, and context is the main reason. My runner's context window has to hold everything, meaning my prompt, the conversation history, any files I added, and also the model's thinking. This is an excellent setting to turn up when you have a high temperature (more random than analytical) because it basically prevents the model from going a little off the rails. 1.5TB of model, 350GB of computer. Math shouldn't work like this.

item.title: These AI-made Adobe clones finally freed me from dual-booting Windows for good
item.itunes:title: These AI-made Adobe clones finally freed me from dual-booting Windows for good
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For as long as Linux has been my main desktop, my boot menu has had a second entry that existed mostly for Adobe. If I need to work with a .psd template, edit some product shots for a review, or cut a quick video, I'm almost exclusively doing it in Windows because that's where the Adobe tools I pay for are. There simply hasn't been a Linux equivalent that can match the workflow that has been engrained in me by the Creative Cloud suite. That is, until now.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

When ArtCraft released its suite of what it calls "crafting apps," users called them what they were on the surface: Adobe clones. They're free, open-source reimplementations of Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro, written in Rust with help from Claude Opus. While they reportedly work well on Windows and macOS, they're also compatible with Linux. They're certainly not perfect, but I haven't booted Windows for work since, and for the kind of work that I do on a daily basis, I think that's indicative of how close they can get.

An open-source Adobe suite built with AI is almost ready to replace the real thing

ArtCraft has seriously impressed me

6
By  Ty Sherback

They're all native Linux apps

There's no emulation layer or workaround here

When I first installed these apps on my system, the thing that stood out instantly was how quickly they booted, and how everything worked on the first go. These apps have native Linux builds that ship as AppImages, but you can also use them as a Flatpak or plain binary if that's more your style. On my CachyOS system with a GNOME desktop, I just went with the AppImage.

The biggest difference between these apps and the native creative apps Linux has had for years is familiarity. GIMP, Krita, darktable, and Kdenlive can all do serious work, but each asks you to learn its own way of doing things, and some of them are a lot more workable than others. The ArtCraft apps copy Adobe's layouts on purpose, and the ones I use most often, like Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and Lightroom, all now have a Linux equivalent that has a UI that recreates the experience of using them to a tee.

For example, in FilmCraft, all the same keyboard shortcuts, workspaces and panels within are pretty much 1:1 with Adobe. There are even keyboard presets for Final Cut Pro and Avid, so if you're coming from either of those, you should feel at home.

I replaced the Adobe suite with a free open source alternative that Claude can control directly

Artcraft clones Adobe's apps for free, and Claude can run them for you.

9
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Most of my files actually open

There are some exceptions, but compatibility is pretty good

Running natively only matters if your work comes with you, and for the most part, mine did. My layered PSDs with Photoshop came through to PhotoCraft almost 1:1, with all the masks and adjustments recreated perfectly. PdfCraft opened everything I sent to it first try, and surprisingly, the in-progress After Effects projects I had managed to open in EffectCraft, though I think that's probably because not much work had been done in them to that point. LightCraft also not only opened the RAW files from my Canon T3i just fine, but it opened my Lightroom Classic catalog file instantly on the first go.

5 reasons why I'm moving my photo and video editing to free, open-source, and self‑hosted tools

I ditched bloated and pricy creative apps for tools I can actually control

14
By  Nolen Jonker

The ArtCraft apps aren't fully-featured yet

Alpha software comes with alpha problems

These apps definitely have their rough edges, but that's not exclusive to the Linux versions. Every app in the suite is currently labeled as "in development." There are plenty of GitHub issues that report issues with the entire suite, so it's definitely the case that these are a volatile work-in-progress.

The biggest gap for my use case is Premiere, because FilmCraft can't open project files that have been created in the native Adobe app. Speed is a gap as well, and while I haven't been able to discern any speed difference in my own projects, Scott Simmons

of ProVideo Coalition did some testing in a slightly more complicated environment and found it to be a lot slower in both it's UI and its export time. If you're a working professional and are considering moving to FilmCraft, I probably wouldn't until it matures. That description also fits the other apps; for the weekend creative, these apps are probably enough, but for the professional who needs their tools to be sharp, keeping the Creative Cloud subscription makes sense.

This open-source tool combines Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and After Effects - And it replaced all three for me

I didn't expect it to replace my entire Adobe setup

13
By  Nolen Jonker

The bar for Linux is much lower

Windows and macOS are tough competition, but more options on Linux will never be bad

Most Linux users aren't asking for something that beats Adobe, but moreso something that acts like Adobe. And thanks to all of these apps being free and open-source, even with legal takedowns, users can fork and continue to develop the apps. ArtCraft calls these clean-room reimplementations, meaning they recreate Adobe’s functionality without using its code or assets, but nobody knows yet how Adobe’s patents apply to an AI-assisted rebuild of its apps. If the project does run into legal trouble, the open-source license at least means the code can’t simply disappear, even if forks wouldn’t be immune to the same sort of challenge.

The spread is already taking place; PhotoCraft’s code was reused to build PhotoSuite, another free image editor, and other clones are being made as I write this. The development on these applications is moving so fast that the version that I'm using in these articles will likely be outdated by the time you're reading this. I wouldn't go as far as to say that they're better than the options already available on Linux, but for someone like me, who has basically only ever worked in Adobe and doesn't want to learn anything new, these apps are a lifesaver, even in their half-finished state.

item.title: Moving my Wi-Fi 6 router to a shelf beat my $330 Wi-Fi 7 upgrade in the bedroom
item.itunes:title: Moving my Wi-Fi 6 router to a shelf beat my $330 Wi-Fi 7 upgrade in the bedroom
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Enthusiastic spending often makes us regret it. I recently came across such a case. I had an old Wi-Fi 6 router running a gigabit plan, and the speeds were fine too. But since Wi-Fi 7 kept fantasizing me, I upgraded to TP-Link Archer BE800, a Wi-Fi 7 router. I got it for about $330 during a sale, so I was happy even before seeing any improvement in connection speeds.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Upon testing, at first I ran it under my TV, and my OnePlus 13R showed a 2,882Mbps link to it. Then I ran a speed test, and it said 924Mbps. The surprising part was that my old Wi-Fi 6 router used to manage 917Mbps from the same position, just 7 Mbps short of a Wi-Fi 7 router. Shocked, I kept testing speeds for 12 days, and the verdict was embarrassing.

My gigabit plan was the ceiling all along

Twelve days of speed tests, one very flat table

I tested speeds the boring way, because boring is the only kind of test I trust. I logged five Speedtest runs per spot on my TP-Link Archer AX55 the week before the BE800 arrived, then repeated them on the new router. Again, the same TV cabinet and around 9 p.m., when half my building streams something. Here are the averages.

Download in Mbps (five-run average)

Archer AX55 (Wi-Fi 6)

Archer BE800 (Wi-Fi 7)

Wired, laptop with USB-C adapter

938

939

Desk, MacBook Air M2

803

812

Bedroom, MacBook Air M2

512

547

Desk, OnePlus 13R

917

924

Bedroom, OnePlus 13R

603

688

The wired row shows a gigabit plan at full stretch. Since Ethernet framing and TCP overhead shave about 6% off the top, roughly 940 Mbps is the best any 1Gbps line shows on a speed test. My ISP's fiber box also hands off through a single gigabit port, which means the BE800's 10G WAN port spent its whole stay plugged into a 1G port. Talking wireless: near the router, the OnePlus 13R gained 7 Mbps; with distance, the gap got bigger.

Wi-Fi 7 will not fix what's actually wrong with your home network

A new router alone won't upgrade your network to Wi-Fi 7

1
By  Tanveer Singh

My laptop can't use Wi-Fi 7's big features

One menu tells you before you spend a dime

But the gap still wasn't big enough, especially for my old MacBook Air M2. It never even reached the plan's ceiling, and that's when I realized: it's my laptop, not the internet. Apple's own spec list puts the MacBook Air M2 on Wi-Fi 6 with 80MHz channels and a 1,200 Mbps maximum link rate, and real downloads always land well under the link rate. Option-clicking the Wi-Fi icon showed 802.11ax and a Tx rate of 1,201Mbps on both routers.

Wi-Fi 7's two headline speed features need a Wi-Fi 7 device on the other end. Its 320MHz channels, double Wi-Fi 6's widest, only exist on the 6GHz band, and 4K-QAM packs about 20% more data into each transmission, according to the Wi-Fi Alliance. Apple only lists Wi-Fi 7 on its 2026 laptops, and Windows machines with Intel's AX-series cards are stuck on Wi-Fi 6 or 6E too.

Check your own MacBook before you shop: Click the Wi-Fi icon while holding the Option key, then read PHY Mode. If it says 802.11ax, Wi-Fi 7 has nothing extra to give it.

On Windows, run netsh wlan show interfaces and check the Radio type. 802.11ax means Wi-Fi 6 or 6E, while 802.11be means your laptop can use Wi-Fi 7.

Where a Wi-Fi 7 router earns its price

Mostly on traffic that never leaves your home

Wi-Fi 7's extra headroom pays off on traffic that never touches your ISP, and even there I hit the same wall from a new direction. Copying a 20GB photo folder from my NAS ran at 112 MB/s on both routers, because the NAS has one gigabit port. A fast wireless link needs fast wired gear behind it, which is how multi-gig switches end up on the shopping list.

So here's who I'd tell to buy one. On a multi-gig plan like AT&T Fiber's 2 GIG or 5 GIG tiers, the BE800's 10G WAN port finally has a job. With a 2.5GbE NAS or a gaming PC streaming to a Wi-Fi 7 laptop or handheld, local transfers can run well past a gigabit. A crowded apartment building is a fair case too. Since multi-link operation (MLO, as most techies call it) lets a device hold connections on two bands at once, it helps with steadiness more than raw speed.

And if your router just died, buy Wi-Fi 7 without guilt. The dual-band Archer BE3600 sold for about $80 in an early October deal, which is Wi-Fi 6 money. It skips 6GHz, so there are no 320MHz channels, but on a gigabit plan you'd never notice.

Router placement vs Wi-Fi 7 on a gigabit plan

The placement won, and it wasn't close

The number that kept bugging me was the bedroom. Two walls away, the MacBook got 512Mbps on the AX55 and 547 on the BE800, a gain I could barely feel. So I moved the AX55 out of the TV cabinet (behind my soundbar) and put it on top of the bookshelf, about four feet higher.

The bedroom jumped to 671Mbps on the MacBook and 794 on the OnePlus 13R. For the laptop, that's more than four times the bump Wi-Fi 7 gave me, and it cost ten minutes and a bit of dust. I felt weirdly proud of a router and ashamed of myself for ignoring the oldest advice in router placement.

When a Wi-Fi 7 router is worth it on a gigabit plan

So here's the takeaway for you: if you pay for 2 Gbps or more, own 2.5GbE gear, or need a new router anyway, then Wi-Fi 7 is a good buy. On a gigabit plan with a Wi-Fi 6 laptop, it's not. But in case you have that insect to test it out, do remember that the return window is mostly 14 days long. It's long, but never long enough to keep delaying those boring tests.

item.title: I stopped using ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini for every little task, and my local LLM picked up the slack
item.itunes:title: I stopped using ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini for every little task, and my local LLM picked up the slack
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Unlike subscriptions like Netflix, Spotify, or Apple Music, where paying a monthly fee generally means you can use the service as much as you want, AI subscriptions don't quite work that way. You could be paying $20, or even $100, a month and still find yourself staring at a polite little message telling you that you've hit your usage limit and should come back later.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The irony is that AI is probably one of the most expensive subscriptions you pay for, yet it's also one of the few that can lock you out despite paying for it! This is one of the reasons (among others) I've stopped turning to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini for every little task.

Instead of wasting my limited usage on tasks that barely scratch the surface of what these tools can do, I started handing them off to a local LLM running directly on my devices.

We've gotten a little too comfortable using AI for everything

Not everything needs a powerful AI model

Remember when Googling something was practically a reflex? Whether you had a random question, needed to understand an unfamiliar term, or wanted to settle a debate with a friend, your first instinct was probably to open Google and search for it.

Well, I think AI chatbots have slowly started taking Google's place in that regard. It's unfortunate, but it's true. Instead of typing a question into a search engine and scrolling through even a single result to find an answer, it's often far easier to ask ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or whatever your preferred chatbot is and get a response directly.

It doesn't just stop at questions! We've gotten so comfortable with having AI at our fingertips that turning to a chatbot for even the smallest tasks has become almost second nature. I've seen people turn to AI to decide if their outfit looks good or not!

The problem is that every one of those requests counts toward your usage limits, regardless of whether you're asking AI to solve a complicated problem or simply rephrase a sentence. Beyond the frustration of running into those limits, there's another reason I've started questioning how frequently I rely on cloud-based AI: its environmental impact.

Running powerful AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, and the data centers behind them consume electricity and, in many cases, substantial amounts of water for cooling. As demand for AI continues to grow, so does the infrastructure needed to support it. While I'm certainly not suggesting we should stop using cloud AI altogether, I do think it's worth questioning whether every little task really needs to be sent to a massive data center halfway across the world.

Think about what you're actually using AI for

It's the little things that add up

I know I'm writing this as a journalist, so what I'm about to type after this hurts my soul and doesn't really apply to me on a personal level. But if you aren't a writer, there's a good chance you've become somewhat reliant on using AI for writing help.

I'm not saying you do, or that you shouldn't, but I say this based on the countless conversations I've had with people. Even AI companies frequently use writing-related tasks as examples when demonstrating what their models are capable of.

Now, there are two types of writing tasks you'll see people turn to AI for. One is the full-fledged "write me an SEO article about XYZ" kind, which requires research from the web, fact-checking, and the ability to put together a coherent, well-structured piece. That's the sort of task where having access to a powerful cloud-based model can make a difference.

The other is much simpler. Think rephrasing an awkward sentence, fixing grammatical errors, making an email sound more professional, or shortening a paragraph that's gotten a little too wordy. These tasks don't require extensive research, complex reasoning, or access to the latest information. Do you really need one of the most powerful AI models in the world to handle any of that? I've been using my local LLM as a Grammarly replacement for months!

I use ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Gemini daily — here's the only one worth paying for

One stands above the rest.

16
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Cleaning up existing text is, of course, far from the only example. I'm currently a student, so a lot of my AI usage naturally gravitates toward using it as a tutor. Beyond relying extensively on tools like NotebookLM to study, I also almost always have a chatbot open in another tab so I can ask questions whenever I get stuck on something.

Sometimes, that means asking it to walk me through a particularly confusing concept. Other times, it's something as simple as asking what a term means, requesting another example, or getting a quick explanation of something I didn't quite understand the first time around.

While there are times I need the advanced reasoning capabilities of a powerful cloud-based model, not every question I ask requires that level of intelligence. For straightforward definitions, explanations, and examples, a smaller local LLM can often do the job just fine.

Another example is the relatively simple tasks you might've automated for yourself using AI. For instance, you might have an automation that summarizes your most important emails or gives you a breakdown of what you have going on for the day. Or, you might've built a custom tool specifically for your workflow. I personally have a skill that automatically renames any screenshot I take, giving it a descriptive filename based on what's in the image rather than leaving it with the generic name macOS assigns by default.

While I initially had this working through Claude by building a skill I'd run every time I needed to rename a screenshot, I've since swapped it for a script-based implementation that uses Gemma 4 running locally on my Mac. The end result is essentially the same, except I no longer need to rely on a cloud-based model or use up my Claude usage limits every time I want to rename a screenshot.

I run local LLMs on both my phone and MacBook

Local AI doesn't have to be complicated

While I'd love to use my devices to run local LLMs for more demanding tasks, I'm currently working with a MacBook that has just 8GB of RAM. This means outsourcing the little tasks is pretty much all I can realistically do. I've tried a fair few local LLMs that work well with my devices, but Gemma 4 is what I've ultimately settled on. The smaller variants are lightweight enough to run on my hardware without bringing everything else to a crawl, while still being capable enough to handle most of the everyday tasks I've discussed above.

I particularly enjoy using a local LLM on my phone. The fact that I can open Google AI Edge Gallery just as easily as I'd open ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, and ask it whatever question I have without needing an internet connection or worrying about usage limits, is incredibly convenient

item.title: I gave my old PC two cheap PCIe cards, and it became more powerful than high-end pre-built NAS units
item.itunes:title: I gave my old PC two cheap PCIe cards, and it became more powerful than high-end pre-built NAS units
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Ripping out Windows and replacing it with a lightweight Linux flavor is one of the most common ways to repurpose old but perfectly usable PCs. That said, the Linux distribution in question doesn’t have to be a general-purpose OS laden with UI elements and typical productivity apps. Compared to pre-built Network-Attached Systems and their embedded processors, old tower PCs bearing components from the last 4-5 years tend to pack plenty of firepower – and I say that as someone already using outdated gaming PCs to run ZFS pools within TrueNAS.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

In fact, I’d go so far as to say that I prefer recycling typical ATX systems into makeshift NAS servers, as their extra PCIe slots let me arm them with a bunch of cool devices. The first-gen Ryzen PC that I currently use for experimental NAS projects is a great example, as two cheap PCIe cards were all it needed to stand its ground against expensive pre-built servers.

I armed spare PCIe slots with cheap NVMe adapters, and they were the best quality-of-life upgrade for my PCs

Filling the empty PCIe sockets with NVMe adapters was totally worth it

5
By  Ayush Pande

A 10GbE NIC handles my high-speed NVMe pools

It also adds failover provisions to my setup

When you turn budget-friendly gaming systems into DIY NAS units, you may realize that the 1G Ethernet is a huge bottleneck even for standard HDDs – and that’s precisely what happened when I tried using my freshly-configured TrueNAS PC as is. After all, a 1 gigabit connection has a max transfer limit of 125 MB/s, and once you consider the slight decrease in the speeds due to real-world network overheads, it’s a bit slow for recurring backup tasks. I’ve got a bunch of cheap refurbished HDDs from flea market servers, and even the slower ones among them can hit at least 150 MB/s. With the right caching tools and RAID pools, the speed bottleneck becomes even larger.

Now, you could call me out for going straight for 10GbE cards instead of setting on an affordable 2.5 gigabit connection, but I also have some SSD pools that I use as iSCSI targets for my video-editing and (as wild as may sound) single-player gaming needs. Not to mention, 10G setups are a lot more affordable than they used to be. I initially grabbed a few models of TP Link’s TX401 NIC for a few systems in my arsenal, and barring one instance where I couldn’t get an OPNsense machine to detect their drivers, they’ve served my home lab nodes surprisingly well.

Heck, I’d go so far as to say that I’d still be using one of these “inferior” network cards in my NAS had I not salvaged a dual-10GbE X550-T2 card. Between its solid thermals and failover provisions, it serves my NAS nicely, while the TX401 NICs on my gaming PC and Proxmox nodes let my workstations communicate over 10GbE channels. item.title: My Jellyfin server now has a 24/7 weather channel, and it's pure 90s nostalgia
item.itunes:title: My Jellyfin server now has a 24/7 weather channel, and it's pure 90s nostalgia
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Do you remember the old weather channels from the 80s and 90s? They were dead simple: a basic interface that displayed the relevant information, smooth jazz playing in the background, and only the most rudimentary graphics.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Even though they pale in comparison to modern weather channels, I feel nostalgic every time I see a station like this. In some ways, it's easier to use; I don't have to parse the information or look at fancy animations. I missed that, so I decided to bring that same utility and nostalgia back to my home Jellyfin server.

It was easier than you might expect, and the end results are impressive (to me, anyway). If you lived through that era, or you just have a penchant for retro design choices, adding WeatherStar 4000+ to your Jellyfin server might be your next big project.

The process begins with Docker

Every piece of the puzzle is self-hosted

I used Docker to spin up a container for WeatherStar 4000+. It took next to no time at all; a simple docker-compose.yaml file, and I was off to the races. You don't need Jellyfin to run WeatherStar, either. I wanted to add the station to my home server for fun, but WeatherStar can run independently of Jellyfin. If you're curious what it looks like, you can check it out in action at its website. And if that version isn't retro enough for you, WeatherStar 3000+ takes things back another decade or so.

Once WeatherStar is up and running, you can change most everything about it. It's essentially a slideshow with dynamic conditions, so you can choose which "slides" you want to see and which you don't. For instance, you might ditch "Extended Forecast" if you're only concerned about the next few days. It also offers five speeds (Very Slow, Slow, Normal, Fast, and Very Fast), four display modes, and the option to switch between US and Metric units. You can also turn on Kiosk mode, which enlarges the display and hides the settings menu.

I added live weather radar to Android Auto, and it changed how I plan my drives

Live weather radar in Android Auto solved the one thing forecasts can't tell you.

6
By  Dhruv Bhutani

WeatherStar 4000+ can be turned into a TV channel

Sharing options make it easy to be your own meteorologist

The next step was to broadcast the WeatherStar feed, so it was accessible outside the computer it was hosted on. To do that, I went to the "Share" tab of the settings menu and copied the permalink that appeared there, before editing the docker-compose.yaml file to include the link. Don't let the last step intimidate you; I only had to add a single line and run the file again in the Terminal.

Then I ran ws4channels to transform my browser feed of WeatherStar 4000+ into a functional, active stream. Next, I added the channel to my Jellyfin server. To do that, I signed in to Jellyfin as an administrator and opened Settings > Dashboard > Live TV. Jellyfin allows users to add different tuner devices. I selected the M3U tuner from the dropdown box and pointed it toward the M3U playlist generated by ws4channels. After finishing the setup, WeatherStar 4000+ appeared in my Live TV section of my server.

My weather channel is surprisingly useful

Sometimes simpler really is better

I keep the TV on in the background to fill in the quiet. I've never enjoyed a totally silent home. The problem is that I'm also easily distracted, and a TV show often proves too interesting, tearing my attention away from the task at hand. My WeatherStar channel is a continuous loop with only minor updates as the day wears on. There's no breaking news or talking heads — just smooth jazz, a straightforward presentation of the temperature and forecast, and possibly a live radar.

It combines the best of both worlds: a retro, nostalgic display with up-to-date weather information and forecasts. If there were severe storms in my area, I'd turn to the current news, but for day-to-day armchair meteorology? WeatherStar 4000+ is a great pick.

This Jellyfin plugin made my media library feel like old-school cable TV

This plugin lets me manage my media like my own TV station.

By  Brian Burgess

WeatherStar is fun, but it's not necessarily practical

This isn't the easiest way to check the forecast

Weather used to be something we had to check on a specific channel (at a specific time of day) to learn anything about, but now it's at our fingertips. I have the current temperature and conditions on my watch. They're also visible in the bottom-right corner of my monitor in the taskbar. I can see weather alerts on my phone's home screen, and I have at least three different weather apps downloaded.

All that to say, WeatherStar 4000+ is a fun, enjoyable project, but it's not the most practical way to figure out whether to wear a jacket. There are easier ways. This program exists for people who like to tinker, appreciate retro design, and don't mind spending an hour or so getting everything set up and running properly.

Some things are worth bringing back just for fun

I enjoyed the time I spent setting up WeatherStar 4000+, and it's cool to see and hear something that feels like such a blast from the past. When I check the weather this way, it teleports me back to being a kid, eating cereal at the dining room table and watching the tiny, slightly fuzzy TV in the kitchen.

item.title: Collabora hits back at claims that Denmark ditched it, saying its problems were fixed long ago
item.itunes:title: Collabora hits back at claims that Denmark ditched it, saying its problems were fixed long ago
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Collabora says the reported split with Denmark was false, that it fixed pilot issues, and that collaboration continues.
  • The company claims Collabora engineers resolved initial OOXML bugs at their own expense during the pilot.
  • Collabora says testing paused after a government reshuffle and that the halt was not due to the software's quality.

A week ago, we reported that the Danish government had reportedly cut ties with Collabora. Now, Collabora has released an official statement about the situation.

The company claims the problems have long since been fixed and that it's still working with the Danish government despite the pilot program's pause.

Collabora says the testing phase with the Danish government went well

The trial allowed users to switch between Collabora and Microsoft Office

Credit: Collabora

The situation began when ComputerWorld.de (paywalled) reported that the Danish government was cutting ties with Collabora, citing a report from Version2 (paywalled). In it, ComputerWorld indicated that the trials stopped because Collabora wasn't working properly.

Now, Collabora Online has published a press release in direct response to these claims. The company says that the first testing phase with the Danish government actually went very well, with Collabora working closely with cBrain, which supplies the F2 platform across the Danish government. The trial allowed users to switch between Collabora and Microsoft Office while still using Microsoft's file format.

So what about those problems the Danish government had with Collabora? According to the company, that's actually old news now:

Initial issues with the pilot were leaked to the Danish press in December 2025. Senior Collabora Office engineers investigated and resolved the reported tickets. We were pleased to invest engineering and QA time in supporting the evaluation at our own expense, as we often do to serve our growing number of pilot accounts.

Before the second phase of testing could begin, the Danish government underwent a reshuffle, including abolishing the Ministry of Digitization. This has put the test on hold, which Collabora says wasn't due to any quality issues. The pause doesn't mean Collabora's rollout has halted entirely, as the company claims it's using what it learned alongside cBrain to roll out the software to other Danish public authorities.
